paraphrase: When an ordinary person praises the Tathāgata, it is only for trifling matters of mere virtue — abstaining from killing, stealing, unchastity, false and harsh speech, and from the many kinds of low arts, divination and luxury listed in the short, middle and long sections on virtue.

paraphrase: Ascetics and brahmins who theorise about the past and the future do so on sixty-two grounds: eternalism, partial eternalism, the world as finite or infinite, evasive 'eel-wriggling', chance origination (eighteen about the past); the self after death as percipient, non-percipient or neither, annihilationism, and nibbāna here and now identified with sense-pleasure or the jhānas (forty-four about the future).

paraphrase: Those views are only the feeling of those who do not know and see, the agitation and writhing of those sunk in craving; they are conditioned by contact, and none of them could be experienced without contact. Those theorists experience them through the six fields of contact, and with feeling as condition comes craving, clinging, becoming, birth, ageing and death. The Tathāgata knows these grounds, their destiny and what lies beyond them, and is freed without clinging.

paraphrase: All these theorists are caught in this net as the fish of a pond in a fine-meshed net. The Tathāgata's body stands with the cord that leads to becoming cut; while the body lasts gods and humans see him, at its breaking up they will not — as mangoes follow a stalk that is cut.

paraphrase: Ajātasattu reports the answers of the six teachers: Pūraṇa Kassapa's doctrine that there is no evil or merit in deeds (non-action), Makkhali Gosāla's purification through wandering on in saṃsāra by fate, Ajita Kesakambalī's annihilationism (nothing survives death), Pakudha Kaccāyana's seven unmade bodies, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta's fourfold restraint and Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta's evasion; each answered a question about fruits with something else.

paraphrase: Resorting to a secluded dwelling, sitting cross-legged with mindfulness established, he cleanses his mind of covetousness, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. The five hindrances are like a debt, a disease, a prison, slavery and a desert journey; their abandoning is like freedom from debt, health, release, emancipation and reaching safety — and on seeing them abandoned, gladness and joy arise.

paraphrase: There is a path — the noble eightfold path — by which one sees for oneself that the Buddha speaks at the right time and truly. paraphrase: Perceptions arise and cease with a cause: by training some perceptions arise and some cease. Through the gradual training the monk passes from perception to perception through the jhānas and formless states; at the peak of perception he neither intends nor wills, and so perceptions cease and he touches cessation — the progressive cessation of perception attained with full awareness.

paraphrase: Asked whether perception is a person's self, the Buddha shows that for any self one posits — gross, mind-made or formless — perception would be one thing and self another; and he declines to declare whether the world is eternal or the Tathāgata exists after death, because these are not beneficial, not the basis of the holy life, and do not lead to disenchantment and nibbāna; what he has declared is the four noble truths.

paraphrase: A monk asked the gods in turn, up to Great Brahmā, where earth, water, fire and air cease without remainder; Brahmā, unable to answer, sent him to the Buddha, who said the question should be where the elements, long and short, fine and coarse, name and form find no footing — answered: in consciousness that does not manifest, infinite, radiant all round; there, with the cessation of consciousness, all this ceases.

paraphrase: Ways of describing a self: as having form or formless, limited or infinite; and ways of regarding self: 'feeling is my self', 'my self is without feeling', 'my self feels'. Each is examined: feeling is impermanent, conditioned and liable to cease, so taking it as self leads to 'my self has vanished'. A monk who regards no self clings to nothing in the world and is personally extinguished; of him it does not fit to say that he exists or does not exist after death.

The path to abandoning the five lower fetters: with the first jhāna (or higher attainment) one regards whatever exists there of form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness as impermanent, suffering, a disease, empty, not-self, turns the mind away to the deathless element, and attains the destruction of the effluents or non-return.

The Tathāgata has put away speculative views; what he has seen is: such is form, its origin, its passing away … such is consciousness; therefore he is liberated through not clinging, with the destruction of all conceivings and 'I-making'.

So the form (and feeling, perception, formations, consciousness) by which one might describe the Tathāgata has been abandoned, cut off at the root; liberated from reckoning by form, he is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom like the ocean.

original.text: “Evameva kho, vaccha, yena rūpena tathāgataṁ paññāpayamāno paññāpeyya taṁ rūpaṁ tathāgatassa pahīnaṁ ucchinnamūlaṁ tālāvatthukataṁ anabhāvaṅkataṁ āyatiṁ anuppādadhammaṁ. Rūpasaṅkhayavimutto kho, vaccha, tathāgato gambhīro appameyyo duppariyogāḷho— seyyathāpi mahāsamuddo. Upapajjatīti na upeti, na upapajjatīti na upeti, upapajjati ca na ca upapajjatīti na upeti, neva upapajjati na na upapajjatīti na upeti. Yāya vedanāya tathāgataṁ paññāpayamāno paññāpeyya sā vedanā tathāgatassa pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṅkatā āyatiṁ anuppādadhammā. Vedanāsaṅkhayavimutto kho, vaccha, tathāgato gambhīro appameyyo duppariyogāḷho— seyyathāpi mahāsamuddo. Upapajjatīti na upeti, na upapajjatīti na upeti, upapajjati ca na ca upapajjatīti na upeti, neva upapajjati na na upapajjatīti na upeti. Yāya saññāya tathāgataṁ paññāpayamāno paññāpeyya sā saññā tathāgatassa pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṅkatā āyatiṁ anuppādadhammā.

paraphrase: The preservation of truth: a person with faith says 'this is my faith' but does not conclude 'only this is true, anything else is wrong'; the same for approval, oral tradition, reasoned reflection and acceptance of a view. Awakening to truth: examining a teacher for greed, hatred and delusion, placing faith, approaching, listening, memorising, examining meaning, pondering, willing, weighing and striving, one realises the ultimate truth with the body; repeated cultivation of these is the final arrival at truth.

paraphrase: Among grasses, trees, insects, snakes, fish and birds the marks of species differ by birth, but among humans there is no such difference; the distinction is by designation. Whoever lives by farming is a farmer, by trade a merchant, and so on; I call him a brahmin who has cut all fetters, who is without clinging, patient, free of lust — one is a brahmin not by birth but by deeds (kamma).

paraphrase: The Nigaṇṭhas hold that whatever a person feels is due to past deeds, so by burning away old deeds with austerity and doing no new ones all suffering will be exhausted. Asked whether they know they existed before, did evil, and how much remains, they cannot answer; if pleasure and pain were caused by past deeds, the Nigaṇṭhas who now feel severe pain must have done evil deeds. Their striving is fruitless.

paraphrase: How striving is fruitful: a monk does not overwhelm himself with pain, nor reject righteous pleasure; knowing that the source of suffering is craving, he develops equanimity toward it, or striving, as an arrow-smith straightens a shaft by heat only until it is straight; then the gradual training up to the destruction of the effluents.

paraphrase: In this Dhamma and discipline there is gradual training: first restraint by the Pātimokkha, then sense restraint, moderation in eating, wakefulness, mindfulness and clear comprehension, a secluded resting place, abandoning the hindrances, the four jhānas. paraphrase: For a fortnight Sāriputta saw insight into states one by one as they occurred: in the first jhāna applied and sustained thought, rapture, bliss, unification of mind, contact, feeling, perception, volition, mind, zeal, decision, energy, mindfulness, equanimity and attention were defined; he knew them arising, present and disappearing — and so on through the attainments to cessation, from which he emerged mindful. He is the Buddha's true son, born of the Dhamma.

paraphrase: Noble right concentration is unification of mind supported by the other seven path factors. Right view comes first: of each factor there is a mundane kind, affected by effluents, siding with merit and ripening in attachment, and a noble, supramundane kind that is a factor of the path; right view, effort and mindfulness circle around each factor. The trainee has eight factors; the arahant ten, with right knowledge and right liberation.

paraphrase: The monk, gone to the forest, the root of a tree or an empty hut, sits cross-legged, body erect, mindfulness established, and ever mindful breathes in and out: knowing long and short breaths; training to breathe experiencing the whole body, calming the bodily formation; experiencing rapture, bliss, the mental formation, calming the mental formation; experiencing the mind, gladdening it, concentrating it, liberating it; contemplating impermanence, fading away, cessation and relinquishment — the sixteen steps.

paraphrase: When the four establishments of mindfulness are developed, the seven factors of awakening arise in sequence — mindfulness, investigation of dhammas, energy, rapture, tranquillity, concentration, equanimity — each supported by seclusion, dispassion and cessation, ripening in relinquishment; so developed they fulfil true knowledge and liberation.

paraphrase: Nandaka questions the nuns: are the eye, forms, eye-consciousness permanent or impermanent? like a lamp whose oil, wick and flame are all impermanent, so its light; like a butcher separating skin and flesh with a sharp knife, so noble wisdom severs the defilements. paraphrase: If anyone says 'the eye is self' that is not tenable, for the arising and passing of the eye are discerned; if it were self it would follow that 'my self arises and passes away'. So for forms, eye-consciousness, contact, feeling and craving, and for all six senses.

paraphrase: Pleasant feeling left to itself brings the underlying tendency to lust, painful feeling that to aversion, neutral feeling that to ignorance; that one could make an end of suffering here and now without abandoning these is impossible; seeing thus one becomes disenchanted and is liberated.

paraphrase: Pārāsariya teaches not seeing forms with the eye; then the blind and deaf would be developed. The noble development: when the agreeable, disagreeable or both arise, one understands 'this is conditioned, gross, dependently arisen; this is peaceful, sublime — equanimity', and they cease as quickly as an eyelid blinks; the trainee is repelled by them, the noble one with developed faculties abides perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive and vice versa, or equanimous.

paraphrase: It is impossible that one accomplished in view should treat any formation as permanent, pleasant or self, kill his mother, father or an arahant, shed a Tathāgata's blood or split the Saṅgha, or acknowledge another teacher; impossible that two Buddhas arise in one world-system at once; impossible that a woman should be an arahant fully awakened Buddha, a wheel-turning monarch, Sakka, Māra or Brahmā; impossible that bad conduct should ripen as pleasant.

paraphrase: The seer Rohitassa, able to stride from ocean to ocean, walked for a hundred years to reach the end of the world and died without reaching it. paraphrase: Having awakened, the Buddha reflects that the Dhamma, going against the stream, is hard for those delighting in attachment to see, and inclines to inaction; Brahmā Sahampati appears and implores him: there are beings with little dust in their eyes who will understand. paraphrase: What is dependent origination? With ignorance as condition, formations; with formations, consciousness; name-and-form; the six sense bases; contact; feeling; craving; clinging; becoming; birth; ageing and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief and despair: thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, formations cease … thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.

original.text: “Katamo ca, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppādo? Avijjāpaccayā, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā; saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṁ; viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṁ; nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṁ; saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso; phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā; taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṁ; upādānapaccayā bhavo; bhavapaccayā jāti; jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṁ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā sambhavanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti. Ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppādo. Avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho; saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho; viññāṇanirodhā nāmarūpanirodho; nāmarūpanirodhā saḷāyatananirodho; saḷāyatananirodhā phassanirodho; phassanirodhā vedanānirodho; vedanānirodhā taṇhānirodho; taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho; bhavanirodhā jātinirodho; jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇaṁ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā nirujjhanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti. Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṁ abhinandunti. Paṭhamaṁ.

paraphrase: This world mostly depends on the duality of existence and non-existence. For one who sees the origin of the world as it is with right wisdom, there is no 'non-existence' regarding the world; for one who sees its cessation, no 'existence'. Not taking up the notion 'my self', he has no doubt that what arises is only suffering arising and what ceases is suffering ceasing; this is right view — the middle teaching of dependent origination.

paraphrase: Whether Tathāgatas arise or not, that element stands — the stableness of the Dhamma, the fixed course of the Dhamma, specific conditionality: with birth as condition, ageing and death; a Tathāgata awakens to it and teaches it. What is dependently arisen is impermanent, conditioned, subject to destruction and cessation; the noble disciple who has seen this does not run back into the past asking 'did I exist?'

paraphrase: When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.

paraphrase: The destruction of the effluents is for one who knows and sees; it has knowledge of destruction as proximate cause, which has liberation, which has dispassion, disenchantment, knowledge and vision of things as they are, concentration, happiness, tranquillity, rapture, gladness and faith, and faith has suffering as proximate cause; suffering has birth, and so back to ignorance. As rain on a mountain fills the clefts, pools, lakes, rivers and the ocean, so each stage fills the next.

paraphrase: It would be better for the uninstructed to take the body as self than the mind, for the body may last a hundred years, while what is called mind, thought or consciousness arises as one thing and ceases as another by day and by night, as a monkey roaming the forest seizes one branch, lets it go and seizes another. paraphrase: Edible food is to be regarded as a couple eating their son's flesh to cross a desert; contact like a flayed cow attacked by creatures wherever it stands; mental volition like a charcoal pit into which a man is dragged; consciousness like a criminal struck morning, noon and evening by a hundred spears. When each nutriment is fully understood, the lust for the five cords of sensuality, the three feelings, the three cravings and name-and-form are fully understood.

paraphrase: Before his awakening the bodhisatta reflected: with what existing does ageing and death exist? — and by wise attention came to the insight 'birth', down to 'consciousness turns back from name-and-form and goes no further'. paraphrase: Vacchagotta asks 'is there a self?' and 'is there no self?' and the Buddha is silent. paraphrase: The nutriment for sensual desire is unwise attention to the sign of the beautiful; for ill will to the sign of the repulsive; for dullness and drowsiness to discontent, lethargy, lazy stretching, sleepiness after meals and sluggishness of mind; for restlessness and remorse to unsettledness of mind; for doubt to things that are the basis for doubt. paraphrase: The noble truth of suffering: birth, ageing, illness and death are suffering; union with the disliked, separation from the liked, not getting what one wants is suffering; in brief the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. The origin: craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there — craving for sensual pleasures, for becoming, for non-becoming. The cessation: the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, giving it up, release, non-attachment. The way: the noble eightfold path.

Idaṁ kho pana, bhikkhave, dukkhasamudayaṁ ariyasaccaṁ— yāyaṁ taṇhā ponobbhavikā nandirāgasahagatā tatratatrābhinandinī, seyyathidaṁ— kāmataṇhā, bhavataṇhā, vibhavataṇhā. paraphrase: The conditioned has three characteristics: arising is discerned, vanishing is discerned, and alteration of what stands is discerned. The unconditioned has three characteristics: no arising is discerned, no vanishing is discerned, no alteration of what stands is discerned.

original.text: “Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, acinteyyāni, na cintetabbāni; yāni cintento ummādassa vighātassa bhāgī assa. Katamāni cattāri? paraphrase: When a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata ('he is an arahant, fully awakened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct …'), the Dhamma ('well proclaimed, visible here and now …'), the Saṅgha ('practising the good way … the four pairs of persons'), his own virtue, his own generosity and the deities, his mind is not obsessed by lust, hatred or delusion; gladness, rapture, tranquillity, happiness and concentration arise — he dwells balanced among the unbalanced, having entered the stream of Dhamma.

paraphrase: Monks who develop mindfulness of death thinking 'may I live a day', 'a meal', 'while I chew a few mouthfuls' dwell negligently; those who think 'may I live for the time of one breath in and out, that I may attend to the Buddha's teaching' dwell diligently and develop it keenly for the destruction of the effluents. Mindfulness of death merges in the deathless and culminates in the deathless.

paraphrase: Soṇa strove so hard in walking meditation that his feet bled, and thought of returning to lay life; the Buddha asked whether his lute sounded well when the strings were too tight or too slack — only when evenly tuned. So too much energy leads to restlessness, too little to laziness: determine on evenness of energy, balance the faculties. Soṇa did so and became an arahant.

paraphrase: It is intention (cetanā), monks, that I call kamma; having intended, one acts by body, speech and mind.

paraphrase: To overcome drowsiness Moggallāna should not attend to the perception that brings it, reflect on the Dhamma, recite it, pull his ears and rub his limbs, get up and wash his eyes and look at the stars, attend to the perception of light, walk back and forth with senses turned inward, or lie down mindfully intending to rise. He should not go among families with conceit, nor engage in contentious talk; in brief, 'nothing is worth clinging to'.

paraphrase: Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain turn around the world and the world turns around them; they come to the uninstructed and the noble disciple alike, but the uninstructed is attracted by the desirable and repelled by the undesirable and is not freed from suffering, while the noble disciple reflects that they are impermanent and does not cling.

paraphrase: Anuruddha thought: this Dhamma is for one of few wishes, content, secluded, energetic, mindful, concentrated, wise; the Buddha adds the eighth: this Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation.

paraphrase: Going for refuge to the Buddha, Dhamma and Saṅgha are three streams of merit; abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying and intoxicants are five great gifts, primal and undisputed, by which one gives fearlessness, non-enmity and non-oppression to countless beings and shares in them.

paraphrase: Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī three times asks the Buddha at Kapilavatthu that women may go forth, and is refused; with shaven head and yellow robes she follows him to Vesālī with other Sakyan women; Ānanda intercedes, asking whether women who go forth can realise stream-entry up to arahantship — they can — and reminds the Buddha that she was his foster-mother; the Buddha grants going forth if she accepts eight principles of respect.

paraphrase: Whatever qualities you know lead to passion not dispassion, bondage not release, accumulation not dismantling, many wishes not few, discontent not contentment, company not seclusion, laziness not energy, being burdensome not unburdensome — these are not the Dhamma, not the discipline, not the Teacher's instruction; their opposites are.

paraphrase: Four things lead to a householder's welfare in this life: accomplishment in initiative, in protection of wealth, in good friendship and in balanced living (with four inlets and drains of wealth); four lead to welfare in future lives: accomplishment in faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom.

paraphrase: The uposatha with eight factors: for this day and night the lay follower, like the arahants, abstains from killing, stealing, all sexual activity, lying, intoxicants, eating after midday, entertainments and adornment, and high and luxurious beds; so observed it is of great fruit.

paraphrase: The first jhāna (and each higher attainment up to the sphere of nothingness) is a basis for the destruction of the effluents: whatever there is of form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, one sees as impermanent, suffering, a disease, empty, not-self, turns the mind to the deathless element, and attains the destruction of the effluents or non-return — like an archer training on a straw man.

paraphrase: The ten perceptions: impermanence (of the aggregates), not-self (of the sense bases), unattractiveness (the thirty-one parts of the body), danger (the many diseases of the body), abandoning (of unwholesome thoughts), dispassion and cessation (nibbāna as the peaceful), non-delight in the whole world, impermanence in all formations, and mindfulness of breathing in sixteen steps; on hearing them Girimānanda's illness subsided.

paraphrase: The purpose and benefit of wholesome virtue is non-remorse; of non-remorse, gladness; of gladness, rapture; of rapture, tranquillity; of tranquillity, happiness; of happiness, concentration; of concentration, knowledge and vision of things as they are; of that, disenchantment and dispassion; of these, the knowledge and vision of liberation. So wholesome virtues gradually lead to the highest.

paraphrase: Eleven benefits of the liberation of mind by love: one sleeps well, wakes happily, has no bad dreams, is dear to humans and non-humans, deities protect one, fire, poison and weapons do not harm one, the mind is quickly concentrated, the complexion is serene, one dies unconfused, and if one penetrates no higher one is reborn in the Brahmā world.

paraphrase: Impurity is threefold by body (killing, stealing, sexual misconduct), fourfold by speech (lying, divisive, harsh speech, idle chatter) and threefold by mind (covetousness, ill will, wrong view); purity is the abstention from these — not the rites of water and fire of the western brahmins.

paraphrase: Kamma should be known: its source is contact; its diversity is kamma that leads to hell, the animal realm, the ghost realm, the human world and the deva world; its result is threefold — in this life, the next, or later; its cessation is the cessation of contact; the way is the noble eightfold path.

paraphrase: The eight principles of respect: a nun even a hundred years ordained bows to a monk ordained that day; she does not spend the rains where there is no monk; each fortnight she asks the monks for the uposatha and exhortation; she holds the invitation before both Saṅghas; for a serious offence she undergoes penance before both; a trainee is ordained by both Saṅghas after two years; a nun never abuses a monk; nuns may not admonish monks. If women had not gone forth the holy life would have lasted a thousand years; now it will last five hundred.
